spec.method: Shaken: pour all ingredients into a shaker filled with ice cubes, shake and strain
spec.garnish: Freshly ground nutmeg sprinkled on top
spec.notes: IBA lists this drink as the 'Alexander' (The Unforgettables); its recipe uses cognac, which is the Brandy Alexander. IBA amounts are 30 ml each.

origin.text: The original Alexander was made with gin. In the early 1920s Harry MacElhone, then a bartender at Ciro's in London, is credited with switching to brandy, and the first brandy recipe appears in his 1923 book Harry of Ciro's ABC of Mixing Cocktails.

spec.method: Built: pour directly into the glass over ice and stir gently
spec.notes: IBA calls for 25 ml Drambuie, a little more than ¾ oz (about 0.85 oz). Wikipedia notes the Scotch-to-Drambuie ratio ranges from 1:1 to 2:1.

origin.text: Scotch and Drambuie first appear together in 1937 as the B.I.F., named after the British Industries Fair. It took its 'Rusty Nail' name later: the 21 Club in New York made it popular, the name was cemented by a 1963 New York Times endorsement from Drambuie's chairwoman, and the Rat Pack made it their drink.

spec.method: Shaken: shake everything except the soda with ice, pour into the glass, top with a splash of soda
spec.notes: IBA calls for 10 ml simple syrup, about ⅓ oz.

origin.text: A mid-19th-century classic that appears in Jerry Thomas' 1876 Bar-tenders Guide, written as 'the same as Whiskey Fiz, substituting gin for whiskey.' Wikipedia adds that fizzes were hugely popular in America from 1900 to the 1940s, especially in New Orleans.

spec.method: Stirred: stir well in a mixing glass with ice cubes, strain

origin.text: Created in 1938 by Walter Bergeron, head bartender at what is now the Carousel Bar in the Hotel Monteleone, New Orleans. The name is French for the French Quarter ('old square'). Wikipedia also credits Bergeron at the Monteleone but gives no date and flags the claim as needing a citation.

spec.method: Shaken: shake well with ice, strain
spec.notes: IBA lists it as 'Corpse Reviver #2' (Contemporary Classics). Wikipedia notes the original called for Kina Lillet, now often replaced with Cocchi Americano or Lillet Blanc.

origin.text: The Corpse Reviver #2 comes from Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), from the American Bar at the Savoy Hotel in London. Craddock warned that 'four of these taken in swift succession will unrevive the corpse again.'

origin.text: Created by Hugo Ensslin, head bartender at the Hotel Wallick in New York, and first published in his 1916 book Recipes for Mixed Drinks. The 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book left out the crème de violette, and many later bartenders followed that.

spec.method: Shaken: shake well with ice, strain
spec.notes: IBA does not mention a dry shake.

origin.text: A pre-Prohibition drink named for the Clover Club, a Philadelphia men's club (chartered 1882) that met at the Bellevue-Stratford Hotel. It first appears in a cocktail book under this name in 1910, in Raymond E. Sullivan's The Barkeeper's Manual.

spec.notes: IBA lists it under New Era.

origin.text: Invented by beverage manager Jeffrey Ong at the Aviary Bar of the Kuala Lumpur Hilton, where it debuted on 6 July 1973 as the welcome drink. Its modern form (blackstrap rum, less pineapple) came from Giuseppe González at Painkiller in New York in 2010.

spec.notes: IBA lists it under New Era. Equal parts, 22.5 ml each.

origin.text: Created by Joaquín Simó at Death & Co in New York City in 2011, combining ideas from the Last Word and the Paper Plane. The IBA added it to its official list in 2020.
